text: Seven years after fostering and eventually adopting her dog Kaya from the Evanston Animal Shelter, Jeannie Sanke still returns to Trot for Tails, helping raise funds for the organization each summer. The chow chow, whose photo appeared on one of this year’s event flyers, accompanied the Evanston resident back to the summertime fundraiser, which she said she has attended since 2019. Along with Sanke, hundreds gathered at the Ridgeville Park District on Saturday from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m for the event. EAS, a nonprofit located at 2310 Oakton St., organizes the campaign each year to help cover the growing medical and operational costs of fostering and caring for the city’s animals. Last year, the fundraiser raised more than $35,000 in donations for the shelter. As of Sunday evening, the fundraiser has raised $42,971 in donations. This year, the goal is to raise $50,000, according to EAS Vice President Kate Perschke. Perschke said the fundraising began in February, when the shelter started planning the campaign. To fundraise, Perschke said participants created an online page to collect donations from friends and family before gathering for Saturday’s event. “We’ve had participants raising money over the last five weeks or so,” Perschke said. “Today, it culminates in this fun outdoor festival.” In addition to promoting the fundraiser’s outdoor finale, participants were invited to walk with their dogs in the “Parks Walk,” a morning stroll through 10 parks surrounding the Ridgeville Park District, including Leider Park, Elks Park Tot Lot and Brummel Park. Perschke said the event was an opportunity to highlight the organization’s alumni and sponsors. Some of the sponsors present at the event included the Chicago Stars, Veterinary Emergency Group, Kohn Animal Hospital, EVS Pet Urgent Care, Dogtopia and Corey’s Canine Corner. Corey’s Canine Corner founder Virginia Mann said the organization sponsored Trot for Tails for the first time this year, and she expects to continue supporting it next year. “The Evanston Animal Shelter does a phenomenal job taking care of not only pets, but the people who love them, too,” she said. “They help with custodial care. If your house burns down and you need temporary care for your animals, they help you. That far exceeds what you typically find at a municipal animal shelter.” EAS Executive Director Vicky Pasenko, who has worked at the shelter for about 19 years, said the organization also supports people who adopt animals by helping them keep their pets healthy. Some of the programs EAS implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic include the Community Pet Pantry, which offers pet supplies like free food, leashes, collars and toys to people who cannot afford them. EAS also supports people who need assistance with vaccinations, Pasenko said. One of the shelter’s newest dogs was Frank, a 9-pound Yorkshire terrier found in a park with a matted coat that was stained with urine. Pasenko said the organization meets dogs like Frank all the time. With the donations EAS has received, Pasenko said the shelter was able to take care of Frank, who now has an “adorable haircut” and is “energetic, playful and happy.” “It’s hard not to feel joy when you’re seeing an animal that has had so many problems thrown in his way, and yet he’s happy,” she said. “One of my favorite things about the shelter is animals teach us to be resilient. They don’t worry about what happened last week. They don’t worry about what’s gonna happen tomorrow. They live in this very moment. And that helps us stay grounded.” Since establishing a $7.2 million facility and the city’s first zero on-site carbon emissions building in 2024, Pasenko said the number of animals, especially dogs, sheltered by EAS has increased significantly. She added that in the first half of this year, the organization has taken in 255 animals, which she said is about 30% more than in the first half of last year. Like Sanke, Evanston resident Mike Healy said he fostered and adopted his dog Garnet from EAS. He said he decided to adopt the boxer in 2025 after volunteering for EAS, a connection he said keeps him returning to the fundraiser each year. In the same way, Sanke said adopting an animal from the shelter means supporting an organization that helps all of Cook County. She said what keeps her donating to the organization is witnessing its volunteers, who have helped save more than 97% of the mistreated animals EAS takes in. “I would love to say adopting is all sunshine and roses, but it’s not. It’s an effort,” Sanke said. “It takes time to get to know the dogs, just like getting to know people. The difference is that once you establish that bond with that animal, it’s unconditional and for life. And you don’t just save a dog or a cat. title: Evanston Animal Shelter raises more than $40,000 through Trot for Tails fundraiser
